We’re committing a portion of Anthropic’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new wholly owned entity dedicated entirely to the public benefit.

It will start off with 5% of our shares. For every 50% increase in the company’s value over a set baseline, we can contribute up to an extra 2%, subject to our board’s discretion.

In total, this means that roughly 20% of Anthropic’s shares are committed to the public good. Our co-founders have already pledged to donate 80% of their equity, and around half our employees are donating a portion of their equity as part of a donation matching program we’ve run since our founding.

In the post below, we share more details about our new fund.

items.content:
@spiroskaye @elonmusk I'm definitely not anti-achievement and never criticized real achievements, including by Elon.
I even own two Teslas.

I do expose marketing stunts that, while cool on the surface, are not the achievements they are claimed to be.

Compressed air thrusters might give you acceleration boosts in any direction.
They might even make your car hover for a couple of seconds if you accept replacing the passenger seat by a 400 liter high-pressure air tank.
But they are not a path to actual flying cars.
The same way Burt Rutan's SpaceshipOne was never going to be a path to orbital flights (just bunny hops out of the atmosphere).

I am anti-Musk when it comes to politics. His political actions, the massive dissemination of disinformation through X and other channels, and his support for authoritarian regimes and racist ideas have the effect of weakening democracy and weakening human decency and social progress around the world.

We see our customers upload a massive long tail of complex documents for extraction, which break even the most complex frontier models. 

In order to create a representative benchmark that adheres to this complexity, we invested heavily in a synthetic pipeline that can mine real document templates, but allow flexibility for variation of not only the data, but the template and rendering.

Contrarian Thinking.

items.content:
Contrarian Thinking.

Over and over the contrarians are the ones who change the world. But it is a muscle that needs constant exercise. The masses have the market share and most people hate change.

"I would never share my house with others." AirBnb was born.

"I would never use a digital camera," I heard at Eastman Kodak's booth years ago. Today I shoot all my photos on iPhone.

"I love to drive." Today I often take a Waymo.

"Babies use mice and GUIs." I heard that one in college from a Unix programmer. Now we are headed into a world where we don't use mice and GUIs, thanks to voice systems and brain computer interface companies.

"Art can't be done with AI." Now when you are the Sphere in Las Vegas you are watching a movie dramatically improved with AI.

"Our customers love buttons," engineers at Mercedes Benz said, while pointing out to me that touching screens is more dangerous while driving than touching buttons.

"Cooking with microwaves isn't as good as using an open flame," many chefs have told me. Yet when you arrive home late and need to make something for the kids do you listen to the chefs?

"I'll never use a phone without a physical keyboard," many told me. Yet here we are.

"I'll never use an autofocus camera," many pro photographers told me. Now it is weird if you see a pro manually focusing. 

So, how can you build your contrarian muscle?

Go back to the core problem that humans are trying to solve and rethink it without bias. 

On Friday @broodsugar told the audience at @TheHumanoidHub's event that a Chinese retailer asked themselves "what if humans actually suck at running a retailer." They automated every decision. AI manages every store. Makes every decision of where to put products, and how many to stock, that kind of thing. Sales went up 258%. And this was a well established retailer with billions in sales every year. 

Other ways I was able to get ahead of everyone when I wrote my eight books (I wrote a book about social media before Twitter started). 

1. Learn about bleeding edge tech and ask yourself "what if this got adopted?"

2. Hang around with others who have demonstrated contrarian thinking. 

3. Dream about what the world would look like if your new thing actually worked for everyone. Would the world improve or get worse?

4. Learn some secrets that very few others know. I once talked at Google's first advertiser's conference and they sat me at a VIP table with Kraft food execs. They told me why they advertise and told me how much they spend to acquire a new customer. $34. So when Instagram was bought by Mark Zuckerberg I knew it was an amazing purchase, since Instagram's users were growing exponentially every few weeks. I gave a speech to billionaires that morning who thought it was the stupidest purchase they ever had heard of. It had no sales. No profits. 14 employees. No assets. That is consensus thinking. Which they got into because that's how businesses were (and still are) measured. 

5. Study the problems that people actually are having and then find new ways to solve those problems with fresh eyes. Heck, you can see this in action by visiting @reservoirfarms, that has 20 new companies building farming robots. Every entrepreneur I talked with there spent years walking in farms with farmers, understanding their problems, before they started building robots. I have met many entrepreneurs who worked in weird jobs to learn the industry they are going after. Have you worked on a manufacturing line? In a dentist's office? Or, done landscaping? "First principles" applies to every human endeavor.

6. Learn from Eric Reis. When he was building one of his first companies he spent months building software that he thought people would want. When he launched it no one visited his home page. He learned to test his weird ideas first before he built another thing. 

7. Hang out with people who are different. Years ago I got to hang out with Steve Mann. I shot this photo in 2014, and he had already worn a device on his face for 20 years, even had a screw implanted in his skull so that he could more easily wear a wearable computer. He was weird, let's be honest. Never met someone like him before. But ask yourself "what if he is right, and everyone else is wrong?" There are armies who will tell you they never will wear smart glasses, even today. Can you resist armies who will give you every reason why they never will do the new weird thing?

8. Hang out with the young. I remember being in Hyde Jr. High's first computer club in Cupertino back in 1977. Only five people in it. There were armies of older people (and even many other kids) who would tell me they never would use one and had no need for it. I hung out with @photomatt in San Francisco 20 years ago when he was only 17, and hearing his dreams of how people and companies would publish in the future radically changed my life for the past 20 years. Same for interviewing @VitalikButerin when he was about that age. Laid out an entirely new economics system based on smart contracts. Mullenweg had just started his company and saw a new way for humans to communicate. Today, what, 80% of the Web is running on his software, Wordpress. As much as I hate it, it is rare that people my age (I'm now almost 62) comes up with such a radical shift. It does happen, but far more likely that a 17 year old is gonna build a dramatically important company than I am. Why? They are not burdened by "the way things are done."

9. Ask yourself "is there a better way to do this?" Steve Jobs told his original iPhone team not to hire anyone who worked on a phone at any other company. He didn't want to hear why something wouldn't work, he wanted fresh thinking and new ideas. Back to getting rid of buttons.

10. Question your own assumptions. They might be completely wrong. Mine often are. And be OK with that. I once said that I would wear a Google Glass the rest of my life. That was wrong, obviously. Sometimes I talk myself into points of view that don't turn out to be right. At least short term. (I still am looking for a pair that will make that a right statement). 

11. Build and test with humans who won't blow smoke up your ass (not your friends and family). 

12. Read a lot of books. Anyone who writes a book has thought a LOT about what they are presenting. They often see cracks in consensus thinking. Yeah, often they are science fiction authors, but often not. (I have to take that advice more myself, dropped off my reading). Especially true regarding people who write about new ideas and how to put them into use in business (same here on X, which is why if I find a contrarian thinker I put them on my lists).

13. Remember "experts" are people who got good at building for the masses. But they often have deep blind spots on where the future will be and they often will give you bad advice. 

14. Ask yourself "what if everyone had an autonomous car, a VR headset, a robot, a brain computer interface?" What would be needed that doesn't exist in such a world? 

15. Question your world view. I once was highly religious, went to church three times on Sunday. Thought I was right back then too. And religion is still the dominant world view most people have, but it isn't the only one. Ask most people about autonomous cars and you'll hear religion come back "I'll never let the government look at me while I drive." That's a belief system that person is locked into. 

16. Ask yourself "how could I change even the worst hater?" One "secret" I learned over and over in my career is people change, and even give up religious belief systems, when presented with something new. Henry Ford used to say "if I asked people what they wanted, they answered 'a better horse.'" They couldn't dream of a contraption that would drive them around. Even last night I talked with a Stanford Fellow who gave me the same answer about autonomous cars. He used to run California Microwave, is a very smart guy, but used to have a race car and is stuck in the world view of "I love to drive." 

I could go for quite a while longer, but wanted to open it up to you. 

How do you put contrarian thinking into use in your own life/business or in the things you are building? Are you starting a contarian company? One that, if successful, will force everyone to change?

items.title: Speech AI models that transcribe or translate spoken language sometimes produce hallucinations, flue...
items.content:
Speech AI models that transcribe or translate spoken language sometimes produce hallucinations, fluent and plausible outputs that are not grounded in the audio input. Unlike ordinary transcription mistakes, these fabrications can seriously mislead users and downstream systems. Existing detection methods usually require reference transcriptions or costly manual annotation, which makes them impractical in real deployments, and detection techniques developed for text-only language models do not directly transfer to audio. The article investigates whether the model's internal attention patterns, which describe which parts of the input the model focuses on while generating each word, can be used to spot hallucinations cheaply and automatically.

The authors studied two speech models, Qwen-2-Audio and Voxtral-3B, on automatic speech recognition and speech-to-text translation tasks, using publicly available multilingual datasets covering four languages. They observed that when a model hallucinates, its attention deviates in characteristic ways: it stops tracking the alignment between the audio and the generated text, and attention collapses back to the beginning of the audio input. Building on this insight, they defined four simple measures derived from attention maps and trained lightweight logistic regression classifiers on these features, requiring no reference transcription at inference time. Data for training and evaluation was labelled automatically using word error and semantic similarity thresholds, calibrated against roughly 2,000 human-annotated examples.

items.title: The article addresses a fundamental challenge for LLMs in long-term conversations: maintaining coher...
items.content:
The article addresses a fundamental challenge for LLMs in long-term conversations: maintaining coherent memory across many sessions. Simply enlarging context windows or using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) often introduces noise, loses critical details, and fails to track evolving facts or resolve contradictions. Existing structured memory systems, such as entity-centric graphs, either limit entity classes or overwrite previous information, losing temporal context needed for reasoning. The article introduces APEX-MEM, a conversational memory system that aims to overcome these limitations by combining a property graph with a domain-agnostic ontology, append-only event storage, and a multi-tool retrieval agent that resolves conflicting or evolving information at query time. The objective is to evaluate whether this structured approach improves long-term conversational reasoning compared to state-of-the-art systems.

The approach builds a directed property graph from conversations, where events are first-class citizens and facts are anchored to temporally grounded events. The ontology defines 35 entity classes, and facts include temporal validity intervals and confidence scores. Crucially, storage is append-only, preserving the full evolution of information, including contradictions and revisions, rather than consolidating or overwriting. A retrieval agent uses four tools: SchemaViewer for schema and strategy guidance, EntityLookup for canonicalizing entities and retrieving time-aware fact snapshots, GraphSQL for read-only SQL queries over the graph, and Search for hybrid semantic and lexical retrieval. The system was evaluated on three benchmarks: LOCOMO, LongMemEval, and SealQA-Hard, using LLM-as-a-judge metrics. Construction used Claude Sonnet 4.5 for fact extraction and Claude Haiku 4.5 for entity and property resolution. Question-answering agents were tested with various LLMs, including GPT5 and GPT4o, with a maximum of 40 tool calls.

items.title: Deep research systems, which autonomously retrieve and synthesize information from the web, have bec...
items.content:
Deep research systems, which autonomously retrieve and synthesize information from the web, have become increasingly capable, but they remain largely web-centric. In commercial settings, the information that matters most often sits behind internal systems—customer profiles, order histories, product catalogs—and is reachable only through internal tools. This creates a practical gap: existing deep research benchmarks test web exploration, and existing tool-use benchmarks test whether a system calls the right function, but neither tests whether a system can combine both into a well-grounded, research-style answer. That gap matters now because organizations want to deploy these assistants for real commercial decisions, where an answer that is fluent but unsupported, or that ignores the customer's own data, is worse than useless.

The article's main objective is to close that gap by introducing an evaluation framework, called DeepResearch Retail, for testing deep research systems that use tools in realistic e-commerce settings, and by presenting a multi-agent system, Hybrid-ReAct, as a candidate approach. In short, it asks whether systems can reason jointly over public web content and private, personalized internal data, and it provides a way to measure how well they do so.

items.title: Enterprise IT support conversations are fundamentally diagnostic: users report vague or incomplete s...
items.content:
Enterprise IT support conversations are fundamentally diagnostic: users report vague or incomplete symptoms, and support agents must gather evidence over multiple turns to find an underlying root cause. Standard retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems, which ground language model answers in retrieved documents, handle this poorly. They retrieve documents independently at each turn, so they cannot accumulate evidence, weigh competing explanations, or track which causes remain plausible. This matters now because large enterprises hold hundreds of thousands of historical support tickets, and helping agents resolve issues faster directly affects cost, customer satisfaction, and operational efficiency.

The article introduces and evaluates DQA, a diagnostic question-answering framework for multi-turn IT support. Its objective is to show that explicitly maintaining a diagnostic state across turns — rather than relying on retrieval alone — improves troubleshooting success and reduces the number of turns needed to resolve an issue. The framework treats troubleshooting as progressive reduction of uncertainty over possible root causes.

The article addresses a practical limitation in modern long-context language models, which can read hundreds of thousands of tokens at once but do not automatically know how to connect evidence spread across many documents. This matters for knowledge-intensive multi-hop questions, where the answer requires linking facts from several sources rather than just finding one relevant passage. The article notes that simply putting more documents into the prompt, or using standard retrieval-augmented generation, can improve recall but often leaves the reasoning step weak. The article argues that the missing piece is not more context but a reusable way to structure how evidence is combined.

The article's main objective is to test whether reusable reasoning patterns, called thought templates, can improve long-context language models on multi-hop questions. It introduces a framework named TOTAL, for Thought Template Augmented LCLMs, and evaluates whether these templates help both when the model sees a full corpus and when it sees only retrieved documents.

items.content:
Recommender systems are central to delivering personalized experiences, and a widely used approach predicts what a user will like by learning from the interaction patterns of many users at once. One of the most effective modern techniques in this family, based on a type of neural network called a variational autoencoder, deliberately corrupts each user's interaction history with random masking during training and then trains the model to reconstruct the full history. This masking reliably improves recommendation quality, but until now it was treated as a practical trick with little understanding of why it works or what side effects it causes. The article addresses this gap by studying how information actually flows between users in these models.

The article's main objective is to explain the mechanism by which collaboration between users arises in this class of recommenders, and then to use that understanding to fix a known weakness of masking. It evaluates this both in theory and in practice. The authors first develop an analytical account of when one user's training update helps another user, then propose a new training method and test it on three public recommendation datasets and in a live online experiment on an Amazon streaming platform.

The article addresses a practical problem with LLMs: they often need to be aligned to human preferences, but changing that alignment is costly. Training-time methods require retraining when preferences change, and prompt-based approaches can be expensive at scale. The article argues that users need flexible, fine-grained control at inference time, especially in specialized fields such as medicine, law, and finance, and for multi-domain settings where different audiences need different response styles.

The article's main objective is to introduce and test a method called MEAV, which stands for Model Editing with Alignment Vectors. It asks whether alignment vectors, simple numerical differences between a base model and a preference-aligned version, can represent preference dimensions, and whether several such vectors can be combined to produce diverse multi-domain behavior. The goal is to let users adjust model behavior during inference without retraining or repeated prompt engineering.

Survivorship Bias — How a young statistician identified this cognitive bias and saved lives:

During World War II, the U.S. wanted to add reinforcement armor to specific areas of its planes.

Analysts examined returning bombers, plotted the bullet holes and damage on them (as in the image below), and came to the conclusion that adding armor to the tail, body, and wings would improve their odds of survival.

But a young statistician named Abraham Wald noted that this would be a tragic mistake.

By only plotting data on the planes that returned, they were systematically omitting the data on a critical, informative subset:

The planes that were damaged and unable to return.

The error resulting from systematically focusing on survivors (successes) and ignoring casualties (failures) that causes us to miss the true base rates of survival (the actual probability of success) and arrive at flawed conclusions.

"Vector: A Surprising Story of Space, Time, and Mathematical Transformation"

Amazon description:

A celebration of the seemingly simple idea that allowed us to imagine the world in new dimensions—sparking both controversy and discovery. 

Vector and tensor calculus offers an elegant language for expressing the way things behave in space and time, and Robyn Arianrhod shows how this enabled physicists and mathematicians to think in a brand-new way. These include James Clerk Maxwell when he ushered in the wireless electromagnetic age; Einstein when he predicted the curving of space-time and the existence of gravitational waves; Paul Dirac, when he created quantum field theory; and Emmy Noether, when she connected mathematical symmetry and the conservation of energy. 

It turned out that it’s not just physical quantities and dimensions that vectors and tensors can represent, but other dimensions and other kinds of information, too. This is why physicists and mathematicians can speak of four-dimensional space-time and other higher-dimensional “spaces,” and why you’re likely relying on vectors or tensors whenever you use digital applications such as search engines, GPS, or your mobile phone.

This is why physicists and mathematicians can speak of four-dimensional space-time and other higher-dimensional “spaces,” and why you’re likely relying on vectors or tensors whenever you use digital applications such as search engines, GPS, or your mobile phone.
